unit.title: Python: functions
unit.description: Writing a function with def, calling it, parameters and arguments, return versus print

cards.definition: Runs a function: its name followed by parentheses. Without the parentheses, nothing runs.
cards.example: greet() runs the code inside greet.

cards.definition: A name between the parentheses of def that receives a value each time the function is called.
cards.example: In def double(n):, n is filled in at each call.

cards.definition: The actual value you pass to a function when you call it, between the parentheses.
One only shows a value on the screen; the other sends it back to the code so it can be reused.
cards.example: total = add(2, 3) works only if add sends its result back.

cards.definition: The indented lines under the def line; they run each time the function is called.
cards.example: Everything shifted right under def greet(): belongs to greet.

cards.definition: What a function gives back when it has no return line: the special value meaning nothing.
cards.example: x = print("Hi") stores None in x.

exercises.explain: Defining a function does not run it. Each call, greet(), runs its body once.
whyWrong: The function is called twice, so it runs twice.
A function runs when called, and here it is called twice.
The function prints its text, not its name.

choices: Nothing, because it is never called
Hello, because it runs by itself
hello, the name of the function
An error, as nothing is called
exercises.explain: def only defines the function. To run it, call it with its name and parentheses: hello().
whyWrong: A function never runs by itself: it must be called.
Even when called, it prints its text, not its name.
Defining a function without calling it is allowed.

exercises.explain: The argument 4 goes into the parameter n. return sends back 4 * 2, and print shows it.
whyWrong: 4 is the value passed in; the function sends it back doubled.
The expression is computed with n equal to 4.
print shows the value sent back, not the name.

exercises.prompt: In def greet(name):, what is name?
choices: A parameter: it receives a value at each call
The value sent back by the function
The text shown on the screen
exercises.explain: Parameters are listed between the parentheses of def. greet("Ana") fills name with "Ana".
whyWrong: The value sent back comes from return.
name holds whatever is passed in; it is not shown by itself.
name is an ordinary name chosen by the developer.

exercises.explain: "Mia" is the argument: it fills the parameter name, and return sends back "Hi Mia".
whyWrong: name is replaced by the value passed in, "Mia".
The call runs the function; its code is not printed.
The function adds "Hi " in front of the name.

exercises.prompt: What does the last line print?
exercises.explain: add prints the sum but does not return it, so it gives back None. To reuse a result, use return.
whyWrong: The function never sends its result back, so total holds None.
The function adds 2 and 3, and even that result is not returned.
The code runs: it just stores None.

code.src:
def add(a, b):
    print(a + b)

total = add(2, 3)
print(total)

exercises.prompt: Lines written after return, inside the same function, still run.
exercises.explain: return sends the value back and ends the function at once. The lines below it never run.

exercises.prompt: Build the first line of a function named greet that takes a parameter name.
exercises.explain: def greet(name): the keyword def, the name, the parameters, then a colon. The body is indented below.

exercises.prompt: The script prints None instead of 10. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explain: The sum is computed but never sent back. Without return, a function gives None. Write return a + b.

exercises.prompt: Build the line that calls the function add with the numbers 2 and 3.
exercises.explain: Call a function with its name, then the arguments in parentheses, separated by commas: add(2, 3).

exercises.prompt: Why put code in a function instead of copying it in three places?
choices: To fix it once and reuse it everywhere
To make the script run on more computers
To hide the code from other people
exercises.explain: One function, many calls: a fix inside the function fixes every place that uses it.
whyWrong: Functions organize code; they do not change where it runs.
Code inside a function is just as visible.
Copying is allowed, just much harder to maintain.
